scenarios.title: Before the winter
scenarios.role: A member of a coastal household
scenarios.intro: Autumn is ending. Your group must balance stores, relationships, and knowledge of the shore. This is an imagined situation, not a recovered Jomon conversation.

steps.title: The tide gives you a choice
steps.text: There is time for one substantial task today. What will you prioritize?
steps.low: Supplies are thin; the choice now feels less comfortable.

choices.label: Gather and process food
choices.result: You increase immediate stores, but spend time that could have supported other relationships.

choices.label: Help another household repair its gear
choices.result: There is less food to show tonight, but you strengthen a reciprocal relationship.

choices.label: Explore a different stretch of coast
choices.result: You learn a new resource location. Exploration takes time and does not guarantee an immediate return.

steps.title: Visitors at the hearth
steps.text: A neighboring group arrives while your household is preparing food.
steps.low: Your stores are low, so sharing involves a real sacrifice.

choices.label: Share a portion and exchange news
choices.result: Some food leaves your stores. In return, relationships and environmental information may become more useful.

choices.label: Exchange toolmaking knowledge
choices.result: You focus on a skill exchange rather than a large meal. Cooperation need not require currency.

choices.label: Keep most stores for the household
choices.result: You preserve a buffer, but an opportunity for closer exchange passes.

steps.title: What will tomorrow remember?
steps.text: You want to pass useful knowledge to a younger member of the group.
steps.low: Limited stores make knowledge about reliable resources especially valuable.

choices.label: Practice food processing together
choices.result: Hands-on repetition connects a material skill with the seasons.

choices.label: Visit a neighboring household together
choices.result: You pass on relationships as well as instructions.

choices.label: Revisit the newly explored coast
choices.result: You invest in environmental knowledge whose payoff may arrive later.

scenarios.title: The letter before sunrise
scenarios.intro: A household at court needs a carefully judged reply. Literary skill matters, but so do rank, timing, and the labor that supports elegance.

steps.title: A delicate reply
steps.text: A senior attendant asks for help preparing a response.
steps.low: Your household's resources are limited; even a polished response has material costs.

choices.label: Ask about the relationship first
choices.result: You learn why the recipient and occasion matter before choosing words.

choices.label: Choose elaborate paper and presentation
choices.result: Presentation may signal care, but it consumes valuable material.

choices.label: Prepare a concise draft quickly
choices.result: You conserve supplies and meet the immediate deadline, with less time to investigate nuance.

steps.title: An allusion you do not recognize
steps.text: The proposed poem refers to an older work.
steps.low: A mistake could be socially costly when other resources are scarce.

choices.label: Consult an experienced attendant
choices.result: You acknowledge a gap and draw on a relationship to interpret the reference.

choices.label: Use an allusion you understand well
choices.result: You choose control over display. Familiar material can still be adapted thoughtfully.

choices.label: Ask a peer to work through it together
choices.result: Interpretation becomes cooperative; the peer gains a reason to help again.

steps.title: Who made the polished result possible?
steps.text: The reply is ready, but delivery requires other people's work.
steps.low: There is little room for waste, so coordination matters.

choices.label: Coordinate with the messenger
choices.result: Timely delivery connects literary expression with practical organization.

choices.label: Credit the people who helped
choices.result: You make supporting labor visible and strengthen relationships within the household.

choices.label: Record what you learned for next time
choices.result: You turn this occasion into a resource for future interpretation.

scenarios.title: One field, two claims
scenarios.intro: A cultivator, a steward, and a distant estate holder disagree over obligations. There is no simple map with one owner and one unquestioned right.

steps.title: Before the argument
steps.text: Each party insists that its claim is obvious. How do you begin?
steps.low: A weak resource position makes a prolonged dispute harder to sustain.

choices.label: Collect existing records
choices.result: Documents may clarify obligations, though they also preserve the interests of their creators.

choices.label: Listen separately to the parties
choices.result: You learn how the dispute looks from different positions and create space for negotiation.

choices.label: Inspect the harvest situation
choices.result: Practical conditions reveal what can actually be extracted without undermining cultivation.

steps.title: The immediate payment
steps.text: The steward seeks a payment before all claims have been resolved.
steps.low: The household has little surplus, so every demand has consequences.

choices.label: Negotiate a temporary arrangement
choices.result: A provisional compromise can keep production going without settling every legal issue.

choices.label: Request a formal review
choices.result: You invest in clarifying authority, at the cost of time and resources.

choices.label: Seek support from another interested party
choices.result: A wider network can add influence, but creates new relationships and obligations.

steps.title: Make the outcome usable
steps.text: An agreement that nobody understands may generate another dispute.
steps.low: Limited resources make a repeat conflict especially costly.

choices.label: Write down the obligations
choices.result: A record supports future claims but must still be interpreted and enforced.

choices.label: Explain the arrangement locally
choices.result: Shared understanding makes implementation more plausible.

choices.label: Check the demands against the next harvest
choices.result: You connect formal obligations with the productive limits of the field.

scenarios.title: A print shop on a deadline
scenarios.role: A fictional apprentice in a city shop
scenarios.intro: A new print has customers waiting. Your work depends on craftspeople, suppliers, regulations, and the habits of a crowded city.

steps.title: What will catch attention?
steps.text: The shop needs a subject that can find an audience.
steps.low: Materials are scarce, so a failed edition would hurt.

choices.label: Study what customers ask about
choices.result: Audience knowledge can guide a choice, though demand is never guaranteed.

choices.label: Consult the experienced designer
choices.result: The relationship can improve judgment and quality.

choices.label: Reuse a familiar theme with a new detail
choices.result: You reduce risk and material waste, at the cost of less novelty.

steps.title: A problem with the paper
steps.text: The delivery is smaller than expected.
steps.low: With few supplies left, coordination matters more than speed.

choices.label: Reduce the first print run
choices.result: You conserve materials while learning whether customers respond.

choices.label: Negotiate another delivery
choices.result: A supplier relationship becomes part of the production process.

choices.label: Coordinate carefully with the printer
choices.result: Better preparation may reduce waste without creating more paper.

steps.title: Reading the finished print
steps.text: A customer asks what the image says about city life.
steps.low: Your narrow margin is a reminder that art also has a material economy.

choices.label: Discuss the people and work behind it
choices.result: You connect the visible image with the network that produced it.

choices.label: Explain that it is a selected viewpoint
choices.result: A fashionable image is evidence of representation, not a photograph of every household.

choices.label: Listen to the customer's interpretation
choices.result: Reception can differ from the maker's intention and teach the shop something new.

scenarios.title: A household at a crossroads
scenarios.intro: Schooling and new obligations arrive together. Choices about work and education take place under unequal resources, not in a world of unlimited options.

steps.title: The school day and the workday
steps.text: A child's schooling competes with tasks the household depends on.
steps.low: There is little financial slack to absorb a change.

choices.label: Reorganize work with relatives
choices.result: A network may make attendance possible, while shifting work onto someone else.

choices.label: Prioritize attendance and accept a short-term loss
choices.result: Education may expand future opportunities, but its immediate cost is real.

choices.label: Investigate the school's actual requirements
choices.result: You avoid assuming that national policy operates identically in every locality.

steps.title: An offer from a textile employer
steps.text: A work opportunity could bring cash and take someone away from home.
steps.low: A pressing need for income narrows the room to negotiate.

choices.label: Ask about pay, conditions, and obligations
choices.result: The contract is part of a labor relationship, not merely a wage number.

choices.label: Speak with people who have worked there
choices.result: Experience can reveal details missing from a recruiter's description.

choices.label: Compare the offer with local options
choices.result: The meaning of a choice depends on what alternatives exist.

steps.title: Who bears the adjustment?
steps.text: The household plan distributes new responsibilities.
steps.low: Scarce resources make unpaid work easy to overlook.

choices.label: Make unpaid labor explicit
choices.result: You notice whose education or rest might be sacrificed to support another person's opportunity.

choices.label: Agree on mutual support with relatives
choices.result: A shared plan can spread risks, while creating reciprocal obligations.

choices.label: Keep a record of income and obligations
choices.result: A material record helps distinguish expectations from actual outcomes.

scenarios.title: More than rebuilding
scenarios.intro: A community is deciding what reconstruction should mean. The scenario is a composite, not a simulation of the trauma of a particular disaster.

steps.title: Who is in the room?
steps.text: A planning meeting needs to identify priorities.
steps.low: Funding is limited, so missed needs may be costly later.

choices.label: Invite people whose schedules exclude them
choices.result: Broader participation takes effort and may reveal invisible constraints.

choices.label: Begin with a survey of urgent needs
choices.result: Evidence can improve allocation, provided the survey reaches different households.

choices.label: Repair the most widely used shared facility first
choices.result: An immediate benefit may build confidence, while leaving other needs unresolved.

steps.title: An impressive proposal
steps.text: A large project looks compelling in a presentation.
steps.low: Limited funds heighten the consequences of choosing the wrong priority.

choices.label: Ask who benefits and who pays
choices.result: You examine distribution rather than only the total headline benefit.

choices.label: Compare it with several smaller interventions
choices.result: An alternative may serve different groups more effectively.

choices.label: Organize a discussion with affected residents
choices.result: Legitimacy and local knowledge may improve the decision.

steps.title: Define success
steps.text: The committee needs a way to judge progress.
steps.low: A narrow budget makes honest evaluation especially useful.

choices.label: Measure access as well as construction
choices.result: A completed facility matters only if people can actually use it.

choices.label: Ask residents about livelihoods and social ties
choices.result: Recovery includes relationships and viable lives, not only buildings.

choices.label: Publish what remains unresolved
choices.result: Transparency can sustain accountability without pretending every problem has ended.

phrases: すみません
Sumimasen
Excuse me / sorry
You need to attract a museum attendant's attention.
A flexible polite opener; its function depends on context.
ありがとうございます
Arigato gozaimasu
Thank you (polite)
A guide has helped you understand a display.
The longer form fits a polite interaction with someone you do not know well.
もう一度お願いします
Mo ichido onegai shimasu
Once more, please
You did not catch what the guide said.
The thing to repeat is understood from the situation.
ゆっくりお願いします
Yukkuri onegai shimasu
Slowly, please
Someone is speaking too quickly for you.
A context-dependent request to slow down.
これは何ですか
Kore wa nan desu ka
What is this?
You are looking at an unfamiliar object.
Use the context to make clear what kore refers to.
いつの時代ですか
Itsu no jidai desu ka
What period is it from?
You want to place an artifact on a timeline.
A contemporary question, not a historical quotation.
日本語を勉強しています
Nihongo o benkyo shite imasu
I am studying Japanese
You explain why you are asking for a slower explanation.
A polite statement about your ongoing study.
わかりません
Wakarimasen
I do not understand
You need to make a comprehension problem clear.
Admitting a gap supports learning; pretending understanding does not.
どこですか
Doko desu ka
Where is it?
The place being discussed is clear, but you need its location.
The topic can be supplied explicitly or understood from context.
お先に失礼します
Osaki ni shitsurei shimasu
Excuse me for leaving before you
You leave a workplace while colleagues remain.
Common workplace usage, not a universal goodbye for every situation.
お疲れさまです
Otsukaresama desu
An acknowledgment of shared work
You greet a colleague in a work-related interaction.
Often translated loosely; it is not a literal diagnosis of tiredness.
よろしくお願いします
Yoroshiku onegai shimasu
A context-dependent request for goodwill or cooperation
You begin working with a new collaborator.
There is no one English translation suitable for every use.
